t-beyond.overview: The standard LLM recipe is a tokenized, autoregressive decoder-only transformer: stacked attention and feed-forward blocks, emitting one token at a time. This cluster collects the serious attempts to change one of those assumptions. [State-space models](#c/ssm) and [Mamba](#c/mamba) replace quadratic attention with a fixed-size recurrent state; [Mamba–Transformer hybrids](#c/hybrids) and linear / hybrid attention keep a minority of full-attention layers for precise recall. The [Byte Latent Transformer](#c/blt) removes the tokenizer, [diffusion language models](#c/diffusion-lm) drop left-to-right decoding, and the [Large Concept Model](#c/lcm) and latent reasoning try to think at a level other than tokens. The chat's verdict as of June 2026: hybrids and byte-level models are the most validated at scale, diffusion LMs have shipped but their quality parity is narrow and self-reported, and concept and latent models remain speculative. Historically these alternatives get partly absorbed into the transformer rather than replacing it.

linear-attn.overview: Standard softmax [attention](#c/attention) compares every token with every earlier token, so compute grows quadratically with context and the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) grows with every token. Linear attention reformulates the operation so each layer carries a fixed-size running summary that is updated once per token: cost becomes linear in length and memory stays constant, at the price of lossy recall. Hybrid attention is the pragmatic compromise. Keep full attention in a minority of layers and use the cheap variant everywhere else. [Kimi Linear](#c/kimi-linear), a 48B model, uses full attention (with [MLA](#c/mla)) in only one layer in four and a linear "Delta Attention" in the rest, and reports competitive quality at significantly higher throughput. The open question in the chat is whether a flagship adopts the approach. Like [Mamba–Transformer hybrids](#c/hybrids), it is an efficiency play, not a quality play.
linear-attn.article:
**Linear attention** is a family of replacements for the softmax [attention](#c/attention) at the heart of the [transformer](#c/transformer). It swaps the all-pairs comparison between tokens for a compact running state that is updated once per token. **Hybrid attention** mixes the two: most layers use a cheap linear variant, and a minority keep full attention. As of mid-2026 the hybrid form has shipped in real models, most visibly Moonshot's [Kimi Linear](#c/kimi-linear). Whether it reaches a flagship-scale model is one of the open architecture questions of the next generation.

## How it works

In ordinary attention, each new token's query is scored against the key of every earlier token. The scores go through a softmax and weight a sum of values. That is quadratic in sequence length for a full pass. At generation time every past key and value has to be kept in the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache), which grows without bound and makes long-context decoding [memory-bound](#c/memory-bound).

Linear attention removes the softmax, or approximates it with a kernel feature map, so the computation can be reordered. Instead of comparing the query with every key, the layer keeps a running matrix that accumulates key–value associations. Each new token updates that matrix, and the query reads from it. The per-token cost no longer depends on how long the context is, and the "cache" is one fixed-size state per layer. That is the same shape as a recurrent network, which is why linear attention sits in one family with [state-space models](#c/ssm), RWKV and RetNet.

Newer variants improve how the state is written. Delta-rule designs (the "Delta Attention" in Kimi Linear is one) update the state by correcting what it currently predicts for a key, rather than just adding to it. Gating lets the layer decay old information selectively. These refinements target the classic weakness of linear attention: a fixed-size memory that blurs as it fills.

## Hybrid layouts

Pure linear-attention models tend to lose on tasks that need exact recall of a specific earlier detail. So production designs keep some full attention. In Kimi Linear, one layer in four is full attention (using [Multi-head Latent Attention](#c/mla)) and the other three are linear. Its full-attention blocks also use no positional encoding at all ([NoPE](#c/nope)) and leave positional work to the linear layers, which helps when extending to very long contexts. The same "mostly cheap, a little attention" principle shows up in [Mamba–Transformer hybrids](#c/hybrids), where Jamba's ablations put the sweet spot at roughly one attention layer per five to seven Mamba layers.

## Why it matters

Long context and long reasoning traces are where attention's cost bites hardest, and those are exactly the workloads that have grown fastest. A hybrid shrinks the KV-cache for most of the stack and raises throughput, so the same hardware serves longer contexts or more users. In the chat's taxonomy it is an efficiency technique, quality-neutral by design. It sits alongside [DeepSeek Sparse Attention](#c/dsa), [GQA](#c/gqa) and KV quantization as ways to hold quality while cutting cost.

## Weaknesses and open questions

- **Scale.** Sub-quadratic attention keeps proving itself at small-to-mid scale. Kimi Linear is a 48B model, not a flagship. The chat cites a source calling a flagship adoption (for example, Kimi's own next flagship) "a decisive data point" for production viability.
- **Recall.** A fixed-size state is a lossy summary. The minority of full-attention layers is there to cover precise lookups, and how few you can get away with is still an empirical question.
- **Competition from sparse attention.** Learned sparse attention such as DSA gets similar long-context savings while keeping exact attention over a selected subset of tokens, and it has already spread to a second flagship ([GLM-5](#c/glm-5)).

## From the chat

- Linear / hybrid attention was described as "the most forward-looking direction" among open-model attention designs, with Kimi Linear (1-in-4 full attention, Delta Attention elsewhere) as the example.
- The chat classed it as an efficiency play, alongside MLA, DSA and GQA, rather than a source of quality gains.
- It was listed as the bleeding-edge idea "closest to landing" in a major open model. The caveat: Kimi Linear is only 48B, so frontier-scale viability is unproven.
- When the user asked about simplifying transformer topology, Claude called hybrids "cheaper wiring," not "simpler wiring." They are the pragmatic answer that is winning in production.

ssm.overview: A state-space model (SSM) processes a sequence the way a recurrent network does. It keeps a fixed-size hidden state and updates it as each token arrives, instead of letting every token look back at every other token as [attention](#c/attention) does. The math comes from control theory: a linear system whose state evolves by learned transition matrices, discretized for token sequences. Structured versions such as S4 (2021) can be trained in parallel as a long convolution and run at inference as a cheap recurrence. There is no growing [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache), memory per token is constant, and cost is linear in length. The trade-off is fundamental: the fixed state is a lossy summary, so SSMs struggle with precise recall of arbitrary earlier details. Early SSMs were also weak on discrete, content-rich data like text. [Mamba](#c/mamba) fixed much of that with input-dependent "selective" parameters, and the practical winners are [hybrids](#c/hybrids).
ssm.article:
**State-space models (SSMs)** are the leading attention-free alternative to the [transformer](#c/transformer). They replace the all-pairs token comparison of [attention](#c/attention) with a fixed-size hidden state that rolls forward through the sequence. That makes them a modern, better-engineered return to recurrent networks: linear cost in sequence length, constant memory per generated token, and no [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) that grows with context. The idea has been studied seriously since the early 2020s, and its best-known descendant is [Mamba](#c/mamba).

## How it works

An SSM borrows the classic linear state-space system from control theory. A hidden state vector is updated at each step by a learned transition matrix plus a contribution from the current input, and the output is read from that state. For language, the continuous-time system is discretized so that one step corresponds to one token.

The key engineering insight of the structured SSM line (S4 and successors) was that, because the system is linear and time-invariant, the same model can be computed two ways. During training the whole sequence is processed in parallel as one long convolution, which is GPU-friendly. During generation the model runs as a recurrence: take the state, fold in the next token, emit an output. So SSMs avoid the classic RNN problem of slow sequential training while keeping the RNN's cheap inference.

In the survey framing the chat cited, attention-free models split roughly into those that replace attention with recurrent computation (RWKV, RetNet) and those that use state-space representations (H3, Hyena, Mamba). [Linear attention](#c/linear-attn) ends up mathematically close to the same place.

## Why it matters

Attention's cost grows quadratically with context, and its cache grows with every token. That is the main reason long-context inference is expensive and [memory-bound](#c/memory-bound). An SSM's state does not grow at all, so long sequences cost proportionally rather than quadratically, and serving memory stays flat. The chat called this "a real topological simplification": no all-pairs token interaction, just a state vector rolling forward.

## Weaknesses and open questions

- **Lossy memory.** A fixed-size vector cannot losslessly remember an arbitrarily long past. Attention keeps every token available to look back at; an SSM has to decide what to compress. This shows up as weakness on tasks that need exact recall, such as "what exactly did the token 4,000 positions back say."
- **Discrete, content-rich data.** Early SSMs, whose dynamics did not depend on the input, struggled with text in particular. They could not decide, based on content, what to keep and what to forget. Mamba's "selective" mechanism was designed to fix exactly this.
- **Scale.** The clean quality-parity results are at small-to-mid scale. No pure attention-free model has displaced transformers at the frontier. The field's practical answer is [Mamba–Transformer hybrids](#c/hybrids), which put a minority of attention layers back.
- **Robustness.** A 2026 paper ([Hybrid robustness paper](#c/robustness-paper)) found that hybrids inherit a hidden-state-poisoning vulnerability from their Mamba components. It is early, single-paper evidence, but it suggests the recurrent state is also an attack surface.

## History

Recurrent networks dominated sequence modelling before 2017, then gave way to attention because they trained slowly and forgot long-range information. The structured state-space line (from around 2021) revived recurrence with better parameterizations and parallel training. H3 and Hyena pushed toward language modelling. Mamba (December 2023) made the state input-dependent and was the first attention-free model to match a strong transformer recipe at up to about 1.3B parameters. From 2024 the centre of gravity moved to hybrids such as [Jamba](#c/jamba), [Nemotron-H](#c/nemotron-h) and [Granite 4.0](#c/granite-4).

## From the chat

- SSMs and recurrent models were presented as "the real topology change," the substantive answer to whether the transformer can be simplified.
- Claude stressed that the fixed-size state is fundamental: "you've traded the ability to losslessly look anything up for cheapness."
- Quality-parity claims come mostly from the architectures' own papers and efficiency surveys, which have "a mild optimism bias." Read "matches transformers" as "at the tested scales."
- The frontier-scale verdict (no pure SSM flagship; hybrids winning) was flagged as partly Claude's own synthesis from the trend, and something to re-check.

mamba.overview: Mamba (Gu and Dao, December 2023) is a [state-space model](#c/ssm) whose key change is *selectivity*: the SSM's parameters become functions of the current token, so the model can choose, based on content, what to carry forward in its fixed-size state and what to forget. That fixed the main weakness of earlier SSMs on text. Mamba also simplified the architecture, dropping both [attention](#c/attention) and the separate [feed-forward](#c/ffn) block for one homogeneous selective-SSM block stacked repeatedly, with a hardware-aware parallel scan for training. Its paper reported about 5× higher inference throughput than transformers and linear scaling in sequence length. It was the first attention-free model to match a strong Transformer++ recipe, from about 125M to 1.3B parameters. Pure Mamba has not been shown to match transformers at frontier scale, and it stays weaker at precise recall. Its main legacy is as the cheap layer inside [hybrids](#c/hybrids).
mamba.article:
**Mamba** is a selective [state-space model](#c/ssm) architecture introduced by Albert Gu and Tri Dao in December 2023. It is the most prominent attention-free language model and the most aggressive simplification of the [transformer](#c/transformer) so far. It removes [attention](#c/attention) and also the separate [feed-forward network](#c/ffn), leaving a single block type repeated through the stack. At small-to-mid scale it matched strong transformers. At large scale it has mostly survived as the efficient majority component of [Mamba–Transformer hybrids](#c/hybrids).

## How it works

Like any SSM, a Mamba layer keeps a fixed-size hidden state per channel and updates it once per token, so inference is a single recurrent update with constant memory. There is no [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) that grows with context.

The innovation is **selection**. In earlier structured SSMs the state-transition parameters were fixed, so every token was folded into the state the same way. The model could not decide, based on what a token *says*, whether to remember it or ignore it. Mamba makes key parameters depend on the input. Each token effectively sets its own gates on how strongly it writes into the state and how quickly older content decays. That gives content-based reasoning that earlier SSMs lacked.

Input-dependence breaks the convolution trick that made earlier SSMs fast to train. Mamba compensates with a hardware-aware parallel scan that computes the recurrence efficiently on GPUs without materializing the full state for every position.

Structurally, a transformer block is attention plus FFN. Mamba throws out both and stacks one homogeneous selective-SSM block, which mixes along the sequence and across channels in one unit. In the chat's words, that is exactly the "much simpler wiring": no attention heads and no separate feed-forward layers. A successor, Mamba-2 (2024), recast the layer to connect SSMs more closely with attention and is used in several hybrids, including [Nemotron-H](#c/nemotron-h).

## Evidence so far

- The original paper reported about **5× higher inference throughput** than transformers of similar size, and linear scaling with sequence length.
- It was the first attention-free model to match a strong standard Transformer++ recipe, across models from roughly **125M to 1.3B parameters**, particularly as sequence length grows. At those sizes it matched or beat equal-sized transformers on downstream tasks.
- At larger scale the evidence comes through hybrids. [Jamba](#c/jamba) is about 7/8 Mamba layers and scales to 398B total parameters, and [Granite 4.0](#c/granite-4) and Nemotron-H are shipped hybrid families.

## Weaknesses and open questions

- **Precise recall.** Selection helps, but the fixed-size state is still a lossy summary. Tasks that need exact lookup of arbitrary earlier content favour attention. Hybrids show the weakness where you'd expect it: Jamba exhibits known SSM weaknesses in reasoning and code generation.
- **Frontier scale.** Pure Mamba models have not clearly matched the best transformers at 100×+ the tested scale. The field's revealed preference is to keep a minority of attention layers.
- **Robustness.** A 2026 paper ([Hybrid robustness paper](#c/robustness-paper)) reported that hidden-state-poisoning triggers can collapse hybrids through their Mamba components, including the 52B Jamba-1.7-Mini and Mamba-2-based models like Nemotron, while pure transformers were unaffected. It is one paper on one attack class, but it is a new kind of trade-off.

## Why it matters

Mamba is the existence proof that a structurally simpler network can match transformer quality, at least at the scales tested. It also supplied the building block that made hybrids practical. The broader lesson the chat drew is that the last increment of quality seems to need some attention back. The simplification wins on efficiency, and attention is kept for recall.

## From the chat

- Mamba was called "the standout" of the attention-free family and "the most aggressive simplifier," because it removes both attention and MLP blocks.
- Claude called the small-scale parity real and well replicated, but stressed that it was shown at ≤1.3B parameters. The frontier is "100×+ larger."
- The chat's conclusion: the practical winner is hybrids, not pure Mamba, trading some simplicity back for precise-recall ability.
- Claude flagged its frontier-scale verdict as partly its own synthesis. A pure-Mamba model at frontier scale that held quality would make that read out of date.

hybrids.overview: A Mamba–Transformer hybrid builds most of its [layer stack](#c/layer-stack) from cheap [Mamba](#c/mamba) state-space layers and keeps a small minority of full [attention](#c/attention) layers for the precise recall that a fixed-size state can't provide. [Jamba](#c/jamba)'s ablations found about one attention layer per five to seven Mamba layers to be the sweet spot. More attention improved quality but cost throughput. By 2025–26 this had become a real model class with open weights and published scores: Jamba (up to 398B), NVIDIA's [Nemotron-H](#c/nemotron-h) (8B and 56B), IBM's [Granite 4.0](#c/granite-4) and Tencent's Hunyuan-TurboS. The result is a Pareto win, with comparable quality at lower memory and higher speed, not a strict capability win. Weaknesses remain in reasoning and code, a 2026 paper found a new robustness vulnerability, and many headline comparisons are vendor-reported.
hybrids.article:
**Mamba–Transformer hybrids** are language models that interleave [Mamba](#c/mamba) (selective state-space) layers with a small number of standard [attention](#c/attention) layers. They are the field's practical answer to a question that pure [state-space models](#c/ssm) left open: attention-free layers are much cheaper, but give up just enough precise recall that the frontier won't go all the way. Hybrids keep most of the savings and put back a little attention. Starting with AI21's [Jamba](#c/jamba) in March 2024, they became a shipped, open-weight model class, and they are the most validated alternative to the pure [transformer](#c/transformer) at large scale.

## How it works

A hybrid's [layer stack](#c/layer-stack) is mostly Mamba blocks, which carry a fixed-size recurrent state and cost linear time in sequence length. Every so often there is a full attention block, which can look back exactly at any earlier token. The Mamba layers handle the bulk of sequence mixing cheaply. The attention layers serve as periodic exact-lookup stations. Because only those few layers keep a [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache), the cache is a fraction of a pure transformer's, which is where most of the memory and throughput gain comes from. Many hybrids also use [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) in their feed-forward layers. Jamba does.

**How much attention?** Jamba's ablations gave a notably specific answer. Raising the share of transformer layers (up to 1:1) generally improved benchmark quality but cost efficiency, while more Mamba layers improved throughput. A ratio of **1:5 to 1:7** sat on the Pareto frontier. Jamba itself is about 7/8 Mamba. The frontier hybrids cluster around keeping roughly a sixth of layers as attention. [Linear / hybrid attention](#c/linear-attn) designs like Kimi Linear (1 in 4 full attention) follow the same principle with a different cheap layer.

## Evidence so far

- **Jamba (AI21)** is the largest Mamba-based hybrid family, up to 398B total parameters, with competitive results on standard and long-context benchmarks. Its paper put it roughly level with Mixtral and Llama-2 70B on common-sense and reading tasks.
- **Nemotron-H (NVIDIA)** swapped most attention layers for Mamba blocks to boost throughput. NVIDIA reports that the 8B and 56B family is state-of-the-art in capability with better inference speed, and it was taken through real post-training.
- **Granite 4.0 (IBM, late 2025)** is the most telling size-efficiency claim. Granite-4.0-H-Small outperformed every open-weight model on Stanford HELM's IFEval except Llama 4 Maverick, which is more than twelve times its size. It kept pace on the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard, with sharply lower GPU memory use.
- **Hunyuan-TurboS (Tencent)** is another large-scale Mamba–Transformer design, with adaptive chain-of-thought.

A late-2025 survey named Jamba, Nemotron-H and Hunyuan-TurboS as evidence that the class will stay central as scale grows.

## Weaknesses and open questions

- **Uneven parity.** Quality is comparable on average but not uniformly. Jamba shows known SSM weaknesses in reasoning and code generation. Those are the long-dependency, precise-recall tasks where a compressed state struggles.
- **Robustness.** A 2026 security paper ([Hybrid robustness paper](#c/robustness-paper)) found that hybrids inherit a hidden-state-poisoning vulnerability from their Mamba parts. Even the 52B Jamba-1.7-Mini collapsed on a robustness benchmark, and the weakness extended to Mamba-2 hybrids like Nemotron, while pure transformers were unaffected. It is one early paper, to be held loosely.
- **Self-reported numbers.** The strongest comparisons come from the vendors, on favourable benchmarks (IFEval, function calling). See [Vendor announcements](#c/vendor-claims).
- **Not the overall leader.** The top closed models remain predominantly transformer-based as far as is publicly known. "Frontier-scale" here means large and competitive, not the single best model.

These points are the crux of the contested claim [Hybrids match transformers at large scale](#c/c-hybrid-parity).

## From the chat

- Claude's headline: hybrids have "convincingly demonstrated transformer-comparable quality at large scale with better efficiency," but with "a recurring, specific weakness."
- Granite 4.0 beating models 12× its size on IFEval was called "the standout data point," and Jamba at ~398B "the existence proof at true frontier size."
- It is a Pareto win, not a strict capability win: they keep about 1/6 attention because pure simplification gives up reasoning and code quality.
- The chat cautioned that the Granite and Nemotron comparisons are vendor-selected. Independent confirmation across a broader suite is still needed.

blt.overview: Meta's Byte Latent Transformer (December 2024) removes the [tokenizer](#c/tokenizer). It reads raw bytes and groups them into variable-length *patches* using a small byte-level model's next-byte entropy. Predictable stretches, like the end of a common word, become long cheap patches, and surprising points get their own patch, so compute goes where it is needed, echoing the dynamic allocation of [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe). A small local encoder turns bytes into patch vectors, a large latent [transformer](#c/transformer) works on patches, and a small local decoder expands back to bytes. Meta reports parity with tokenizer-based models such as Llama 3 at 1B–8B parameters. It also opens a new scaling axis: longer patches free compute for a bigger global model at fixed inference cost. Byte models handle spelling and character-level tasks far better. Caveats: the results are self-reported and stop at 8B, not frontier scale. Its sibling, the [Large Concept Model](#c/lcm), goes the other way, up to sentence-level concepts.
blt.article:
The **Byte Latent Transformer (BLT)** is a tokenizer-free language model architecture published by Meta in December 2024. Nearly every LLM first chops text into subword tokens using a fixed vocabulary (see [Tokenizer](#c/tokenizer)). BLT instead learns directly from raw bytes, grouping them on the fly into variable-size patches. Meta reports that it matches tokenizer-based models such as Llama 3 at scales from 1B to 8B parameters. In the chat's ranking it is one of the two most validated alternatives to the standard recipe, alongside the SSM [hybrids](#c/hybrids).

## How it works

Feeding a transformer raw bytes has an obvious problem. Byte sequences are several times longer than token sequences, which worsens [attention](#c/attention)'s quadratic cost and enlarges the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache). BLT gets around this with **entropy-based patching**. A small byte-level language model estimates how surprising each next byte is. Where the next bytes are easy to predict, such as the rest of a common word once its first letters are known, bytes are grouped into a long patch. Where the next byte is uncertain, such as the start of a new word or a number, a new patch begins. The chat put it this way: "a large transformer isn't needed to predict the ending of most words," so compute is allocated dynamically where it is actually needed. That echoes the dynamic compute allocation of [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe).

The model has three pieces:

1. A small **local encoder** that bundles raw bytes into patch representations. It replaces the tokenizer plus [embedding](#c/embedding) table.
2. A large **latent global transformer** that does the main work over the sequence of patches.
3. A small **local decoder** that expands patch representations back into bytes.

## Why it matters

- **No tokenizer artifacts.** A flawed tokenizer distorts input before the model even starts reasoning. The famous symptom is models failing to count the letters in a word, which is a tokenization artifact, not a reasoning failure. Byte-level models do much better on spelling and character-level tasks because they see every character.
- **A new scaling axis.** BLT decouples model size from sequence length. Longer patches save compute that can go to a bigger global transformer at the same inference cost. Meta reports that, for a fixed budget, larger models on longer patches consistently beat smaller models on shorter tokens.
- **Robustness and coverage.** With no fixed vocabulary, there are no out-of-vocabulary words and no vocabulary built around one language's statistics.

## Evidence so far

- Meta's BLT models performed on par with state-of-the-art tokenizer-based models such as Llama 3, tested from **1B to 8B parameters**.
- The line has kept moving. Later work distils existing token-trained models into byte models, retaining over 90% of teacher performance with about a 2–3 point MMLU drop. Other work "byteifies" models to beat subword models on code and character tasks. The chat called this "an active, maturing line, not a one-paper curiosity."

## Weaknesses and open questions

- **Scale.** "Matches at scale" means "at the scales tested." 8B is far from the frontier, and no frontier model is known to be byte-level. The chat's taxonomy puts it alongside the SSM [hybrids](#c/hybrids) as most validated, with [diffusion LMs](#c/diffusion-lm) a tier behind.
- **Self-reported.** The headline parity result comes from Meta's own paper and would benefit from independent replication.
- **Complexity moves, it doesn't vanish.** Tokenization is replaced by a learned patcher and two extra local models. The patching model and entropy thresholds are new design choices with their own failure modes.

BLT was released alongside Meta's [Large Concept Model](#c/lcm), which pushes the other way: from tokens up to sentence-level concepts, where BLT goes down to bytes.

## From the chat

- BLT was presented as the flagship of the most developed alternative line, the one that "kills" the assumption, taken for granted all conversation, that text gets chopped into tokens first.
- In the chat's summary it was placed in the "most validated at scale" tier, "matches Llama 3 to 8B."
- Claude cautioned that "matches Llama 3" is a real but self-reported result from Meta, with some evals only at 8B.
- Some of the sources on BLT's follow-up work postdate Claude's January 2026 cutoff, which is why it leaned on search.

diffusion-lm.overview: A diffusion language model does not write left to right, one token at a time. It starts from a fully masked or noised block and refines every position in parallel over a number of denoising steps, using bidirectional attention because it is editing a whole draft rather than extending a prefix. That parallelism attacks the sequential bottleneck of the [decoding loop](#c/decoding), and it makes long reasoning traces cheaper. Diffusion LMs moved from research to products: [Mercury Coder](#c/mercury) (February 2025) was the first commercial one, and [Gemini Diffusion](#c/gemini-diffusion) roughly matched its autoregressive sibling on coding at about 1,479 tokens/s. Most are now converted from pretrained autoregressive models, and production has converged on [block diffusion](#c/block-diffusion). Caveats: quality parity is shown mainly on code and math, is largely vendor-reported, and a 2026 "No Free Lunch" survey finds speedups shrink under fair comparison.
diffusion-lm.article:
**Diffusion language models (dLLMs)** generate text by iterative denoising instead of autoregressive next-token prediction. The idea is borrowed from image generation. The model starts from a block of fully masked or noised positions and, over a series of refinement steps, fills in and revises all positions in parallel until coherent text emerges. Since 2025 they have gone from research papers to commercial products ([Mercury Coder](#c/mercury), [Gemini Diffusion](#c/gemini-diffusion)). The central claim for them is 5–10× faster generation at comparable quality. That claim is contested; see [Diffusion LMs match autoregressive quality at 5–10× speed](#c/c-diffusion-parity).

## How it works

A standard LLM's [decoding loop](#c/decoding) runs the whole network once per output token, strictly in order. Each step depends on the previous one, so latency grows with output length, and at small batch sizes the hardware is mostly waiting on memory.

A dLLM instead holds a full draft of the output region. In the common *masked* formulation, every position starts as a mask token. At each step the network (still a transformer) predicts all masked positions at once, commits the most confident ones, and re-masks or revises the rest. Because the model refines a whole draft, its attention is **bidirectional**: each position can see both earlier and later positions. A handful of refinement steps can produce many tokens, which is where the throughput comes from.

Text makes this harder than images do. Language is discrete, so the diffusion maths is less natural, and research variants range from masked discrete diffusion to continuous and energy-based approaches (for example, Energy-Based Diffusion Language Models, ICLR 2025).

## Training: mostly conversion

A clear lineage emerged. LLaDA showed dLLMs can be trained from scratch. DiffuLLaMA showed autoregressive models can be *converted*. Dream 7B showed that AR initialization plus targeted training gives the strongest open models. LLaDA 2.0 showed feasibility at 100B scale. The dominant approach now is to start from a pretrained autoregressive transformer and continue training with the diffusion objective, which lowers the cost of entry and explains the recent proliferation.

## Block diffusion

Production designs converged on [block diffusion](#c/block-diffusion): generate in compact blocks (typically 32 tokens), diffusing within each block and proceeding autoregressively across blocks. Like the [Mamba–Transformer hybrids](#c/hybrids), the practical winner is a blend rather than the pure form.

## Evidence so far

- **Mercury Coder** (Inception Labs, February 2025) was the first commercially available dLLM. Inception reports Mercury Coder Mini at 1,109 tokens/s and Small at 737 tokens/s on H100s, 5–10× faster than comparable AR models. **Mercury 2** (February 2026) is reasoning-capable. Inception reports 1,009 tokens/s on a single Blackwell GPU, over 5× faster than Claude 4.5 Haiku Reasoning and GPT-5 Mini, 91.1 on AIME 2025 and 67.3 on LiveCodeBench, but "solid-but-not-frontier-leading" GPQA (73.6) and SciCode (38.4).
- **Gemini Diffusion** (Google, May 2025) generates about 1,479 tokens/s, about 5× faster than Gemini 2.0 Flash Lite. On coding it roughly matches that AR counterpart: HumanEval 89.6% vs 90.2%, MBPP 76.0% vs 75.8%.
- Open weights exist, including LLaDA 8B Instruct (MIT) and Mercury Coder Mini (Apache 2.0), with experimental support in vLLM and Hugging Face.

## Why it matters

The most strategically interesting property is that **reasoning gets cheaper**. The current capability paradigm leans on long chains of thought ([RLVR](#c/rlvr) and test-time compute), and those are exactly what hurts autoregressive latency, since every reasoning token is sequential. If diffusion can fill in those traces in parallel, it attacks the cost structure of reasoning specifically. It is an alternative route to the same goal as [speculative decoding](#c/spec-decoding) and [multi-token prediction](#c/mtp): more than one token per forward pass.

## Weaknesses and open questions

- **Narrow, self-reported parity.** The strongest "matches AR" evidence is in coding and maths, and comes from the vendors themselves. None of these models claims to be the best overall.
- **No free lunch.** A May 2026 survey ([No Free Lunch](#c/no-free-lunch)) compares DLLM inference acceleration against AR-LLMs and finds that the speed advantage carries trade-offs that careful comparison exposes.
- **Structural awkwardness.** Generating fixed-size blocks makes variable-length output and exact stopping awkward. Bidirectional attention also complicates [KV-caching](#c/kv-cache), so much recent work (Fast-dLLM, approximate KV caching) retrofits caching onto a paradigm that doesn't naturally support it.

## From the chat

- Claude's view shifted within the conversation. First it called diffusion LMs "promising but unproven at scale." After searching, it said they are "shipped, commercially available, and demonstrating coding parity with autoregressive models at 5–10× the speed."
- Gemini Diffusion's near-parity with its own AR sibling on coding was called "the single most important data point."
- Claude warned that Mercury 2, LLaDA 2.0 and the "No Free Lunch" survey postdate its January 2026 cutoff, that many sources were promotional or low quality, and that figures like "1,009 tok/s" or "91.1 AIME" should be treated as vendor-reported.
- The verdict: "real, accelerating, no longer dismissible—but not a confirmed transformer-killer."

block-diffusion.overview: Block diffusion is the compromise design that production [diffusion language models](#c/diffusion-lm) converged on. The output is split into compact blocks, typically around 32 tokens. Within each block, all positions are generated in parallel by iterative denoising. Across blocks, generation proceeds left to right, with each new block conditioned on the ones already finished. That keeps most of diffusion's parallel speedup while recovering things autoregressive [decoding](#c/decoding) does naturally. Output can be any length, generation can stop cleanly at a block boundary, and completed blocks can be cached much as a [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) caches a prefix. The chat noted that this is itself a hybrid idea, autoregressive across blocks and diffusion within them. It echoes the [Mamba–Transformer hybrids](#c/hybrids): again the practical answer is a blend, not the pure paradigm. The specific block size is a speed/quality trade-off rather than a settled constant.

lcm.overview: Meta's Large Concept Model (December 2024, released alongside the [Byte Latent Transformer](#c/blt)) takes the opposite direction from byte-level models. Instead of going below tokens, it goes above them. The LCM reasons and generates in a semantic "concept" space, where each concept is roughly a whole-sentence embedding, rather than predicting the next token. A sentence encoder maps text into that space, the model predicts the next concept embedding, and a decoder turns concepts back into text. That replaces the usual token-level [output head](#c/output-head). The appeal is reasoning at a higher level of abstraction, less tied to one language's surface form. In the chat's ranking it is in the "genuinely speculative" tier: an interesting research direction with early evidence and no frontier-scale model shown to match [transformers](#c/transformer). Its claims come from Meta's own work.

latent-reasoning.overview: Latent (or recurrent-depth) reasoning lets a model "think" in its internal hidden state instead of writing out chain-of-thought tokens. Today's reasoning models, trained with [RLVR](#c/rlvr), spend test-time compute by emitting long visible reasoning traces, and each of those tokens costs a full sequential decoding step. Latent approaches instead loop computation internally. A common form reuses a block of layers a variable number of times, so the model can "think longer" on a hard input without producing text. That links it to the older idea of [cross-layer parameter sharing](#c/layer-sharing) and looping, as in the Universal Transformer: the line blurs between a deep [layer stack](#c/layer-stack) and a shallow one run in a loop. The chat held the whole category as promising but early. No frontier-scale latent-reasoning model has been validated as matching transformers, and hidden reasoning is also harder to inspect.

jamba.overview: Jamba is AI21's family of [Mamba–Transformer hybrids](#c/hybrids), first released in March 2024 and the largest Mamba-based hybrid family in the literature, scaling up to 398B total parameters. About 7/8 of its layers are [Mamba](#c/mamba) blocks and the rest are attention, and it also uses [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe). Its ablations produced a notably specific design rule. More attention (up to 1:1) raised benchmark quality but cut throughput, and a ratio of about one attention layer per five to seven Mamba layers sat on the Pareto frontier. Published scores put it roughly level with Mixtral and Llama-2 70B on common-sense and reading tasks. It shows known SSM weaknesses in reasoning and code. A 2026 [robustness paper](#c/robustness-paper) found that the 52B Jamba-1.7-Mini collapsed under hidden-state-poisoning triggers that did not affect pure transformers.

nemotron-h.overview: Nemotron-H is NVIDIA's hybrid model family. It replaced most of a transformer's attention layers with [Mamba](#c/mamba) (Mamba-2) blocks, explicitly to raise inference throughput, and kept a few attention layers for precise recall, the standard [hybrid](#c/hybrids) recipe. The base models come in 8B and 56B sizes, and NVIDIA took them through real post-training to strong instruction-following and long-context results rather than stopping at base-model benchmarks. NVIDIA describes the family as showing that hybrids can be state-of-the-art in capability while offering faster inference. The chat flagged that as a vendor claim, favourably selected. A 2026 [robustness paper](#c/robustness-paper) reported that the hidden-state-poisoning weakness it found in Mamba hybrids extends to Mamba-2-based models like Nemotron. That single early result doesn't show up in capability benchmarks.

granite-4.overview: Granite 4.0 is IBM's late-2025 enterprise model family built on a Mamba–attention [hybrid](#c/hybrids). The chat called it the most telling hybrid data point because it makes a size-efficiency claim, which is the whole point of the architecture. IBM reports that Granite-4.0-H-Small outperformed every open-weight model on Stanford HELM's IFEval instruction-following benchmark except Llama 4 Maverick, a 402B model more than twelve times its size. IBM also reports that it keeps pace with much larger models on the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard v3. Its defining practical feature is much lower GPU memory use than comparable transformers, the payoff of the fixed-size [Mamba](#c/mamba) state. Caveat: these are vendor-reported results on domains (instruction following, tool calling) where the model looks especially good, so they support [Hybrids match transformers at large scale](#c/c-hybrid-parity) without settling it.

mercury.overview: Mercury Coder, from Inception Labs, launched in February 2025 as the first commercially available [diffusion language model](#c/diffusion-lm). Instead of emitting code one token at a time, it refines blocks of tokens in parallel. Inception reports Mercury Coder Mini at about 1,109 tokens/s and Mercury Coder Small at 737 tokens/s on H100s, 5–10× faster than comparable autoregressive models, with coding quality on par. Mercury Coder Mini (1.3B) is open under Apache 2.0. The follow-up Mercury 2 (February 2026) is reasoning-capable. Inception reports 1,009 tokens/s on one Blackwell GPU, 91.1 on AIME 2025 and 67.3 on LiveCodeBench. The chat highlighted Mercury's pitch that long chains of thought become cheap when filled in parallel. All of these figures are vendor-reported and partly postdate the model's knowledge cutoff. See [the parity claim](#c/c-diffusion-parity).

gemini-diffusion.overview: Gemini Diffusion is Google's experimental [diffusion language model](#c/diffusion-lm), announced at Google I/O in May 2025. It generates about 1,479 tokens per second, roughly 5× faster than Gemini 2.0 Flash Lite. On coding benchmarks Google reports near-parity with that autoregressive sibling: HumanEval 89.6% vs 90.2%, and MBPP 76.0% vs 75.8%. The chat called this "the single most important data point" for diffusion LMs, because it is a like-for-like comparison inside one lab. It also marks a frontier lab taking the paradigm seriously. Caveats: the numbers are Google's own, the parity is shown on coding, a structured domain, and the comparison is to a small, fast model rather than a frontier one. It is key evidence for, but not proof of, the contested [parity claim](#c/c-diffusion-parity). Compare [Mercury Coder](#c/mercury).

c-100x.overview: **Claim:** the cost of reaching a *fixed* level of LLM capability falls about 100× per year, halving roughly every two months. The source is [Epoch AI](#c/epoch), measuring the cheapest model that clears a given benchmark bar across all models at their current list prices. The spread is wide: 9× to 900× per year depending on the milestone, with the fastest drops in the most recent year. Two independent analyses push back. The [price-trend paper](#c/price-paper) controls for confounds and finds 5–10× per year for frontier price-for-performance, and only about 3× per year from algorithmic efficiency alone. The [LessWrong open-model analysis](#c/open-price) argues that proprietary vendors rarely cut old models' list prices, which inflates the all-models figure. Open-weight models show a cleaner 7–28× per year. **Status: contested.** A steep decline is real, but ~100× is the upper, confounded end; 5–12× is the more defensible "real" figure. See [cost at a fixed capability](#c/fixed-capability).

c-frontier-fastest.overview: **Claim:** inference prices fall fastest for the most capable models and slowest at the low end. The main evidence is the [price-trend paper](#c/price-paper): models in the top GPQA-Diamond bin fell 31× per year, against 1.7× per year for the bottom bin. Its authors suggest different mechanisms at the top, such as heavier use of [distillation](#c/distillation) and MoE. The explanation is headroom. A newly reached high bar is at first cleared only by one expensive model, so the first cheap match is a huge multiplier. Old low bars have already had their cost wrung out. The main counterweight is the [open-model analysis](#c/open-price), which finds open-weight prices falling fairly uniformly (7–28× per year) across quality levels, and notes that proprietary list-price quirks can distort the picture. Epoch also cautions that the steepest recent rates may not persist. **Status: emerging.** It is also the correction to the intuition that [higher bars take longer to catch](#c/m-harder).

c-squeeze.overview: **Claim:** frontier inference capacity stays scarce, and priced or rationed accordingly, until roughly 2027–28. Support comes from the supply side. [Nvidia](#c/nvidia)'s Jensen Huang sees at least $1 trillion of demand through 2027 and says "we are going to be short," though he sells the chips. [Accuris](#c/accuris) and Tech Insider report HBM sold out for 2026, high-voltage transformer lead times of 36–48 months, and 30–50% of planned 2026 data-center capacity slipping to 2028. The counter is conditional, not contrary. The [Stanford teaching model](#c/stanford-toy), explicitly a pedagogical toy, shows that if demand growth slows to about 100% per year, supply catches up and the gap closes. Claude's own read, flagged as reasoning rather than reporting: premium capacity eases around 2027–28 only if frontier demand decelerates. If reasoning and agentic demand keeps compounding, the squeeze could last longer. **Status: contested** — a forecast, not a measurement. See [Capacity constraint](#c/capacity).

c-incremental.overview: **Claim:** the large, sustained declines in AI cost come mostly from accumulated incremental engineering, punctuated by occasional big ideas that open new room for that grind. The chat's main example is [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe). The idea dates to 1991 and sparse gating to 2017, but almost none of its value arrived then. It came from a decade of fixes: [load-balancing losses](#c/lb-loss), expert-capacity limits, top-1 routing, routing stability, shared experts and systems work for sharding. The second argument is the shape of the curve. [Algorithmic efficiency](#c/algorithmic-progress) improves on a smooth ~3× per year exponential, not a staircase, which is what you'd expect from many small wins. Claude flagged this as its own synthesis, not a claim Epoch makes. Looking forward, it could flip if a paradigm shift such as test-time compute dominates the next phase. **Status: emerging.** Breakthroughs reset the ceiling; incremental work delivers the savings.

c-arch-efficiency.overview: **Claim:** the notable architecture innovations of recent years mostly buy efficiency, meaning the same quality at lower cost, while the big 2025 quality jumps came from post-training with RL and test-time compute. The cleanest evidence is [DeepSeek-V3.2](#c/deepseek-v32). Its only architectural change from V3.1-Terminus was [DeepSeek Sparse Attention](#c/dsa), whose stated goal was to *minimize degradation*, not gain quality. DeepSeek held the recipe fixed and measured parity, with roughly 2–3× faster long-text processing. The capability jump to GPT-5-comparable results came instead from a scalable RL framework and scaled-up [post-training](#c/post-training). The same sorting applies to MLA, GQA, KV quantization, FlashAttention and YaRN: all are engineered to preserve quality while cutting cost. [MoE](#c/moe) sits in between, buying quality per unit of inference cost. [GLM-5](#c/glm-5) fits the pattern: DSA imported for efficiency, with RL infrastructure as the headline. **Status: emerging.** The GPT-5 comparisons are DeepSeek's own.

c-rlvr-new.overview: **Claim:** reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards ([RLVR](#c/rlvr)) gives models genuinely new reasoning ability, not just better use of what the base model could already do. The strongest evidence for it is [DeepSeek-R1](#c/deepseek-r1). RL on a base model produced an "aha moment" in which self-reflection, backtracking and long chains of thought emerged without being taught, and many groups report similar emergence. Against it, a careful [coverage study](#c/rlvr-study) across PPO, [GRPO](#c/grpo) and others found that RLVR raises the probability of correct samples but *narrows* the set of problems the model can solve at all. It sharpens sampling toward answers the base model could already produce, while [distillation](#c/distillation) can transfer genuinely new patterns. The same study found current RLVR algorithms perform similarly and remain far from optimal. **Status: contested.** The chat's read is that the truth is probably in between, and it depends on what counts as "new" and on how capable the base model already was.

c-distill-open.overview: **Claim:** a meaningful share of open models' reasoning gains comes from [distilling](#c/distillation) closed frontier models, meaning training on their outputs. Parts of this are well documented. Distillation from closed models works (TinyGSM trained a 125M model to 63.1% on grade-school math using GPT-3.5 data), and it was pervasive in the 2023–24 open wave: Alpaca, Open Orca, ShareGPT. [Tülu 3](#c/tulu3), the best-documented open post-training recipe, generated its synthetic SFT responses with GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet. The *reasoning*-specific version is weaker. [DeepSeek-R1](#c/deepseek-r1) got its reasoning from [RLVR](#c/rlvr) on its own base model and then distilled that into smaller siblings. No reliable figure for "what share is distillation" exists, because labs don't disclose post-training data and using competitor outputs often breaks terms of service. **Status: contested.** It is plausible and certainly true for chat behaviour, but unmeasured for headline reasoning gains. See [the retraction](#c/r-distill).

c-specialists.overview: **Claim:** a model post-trained only on one domain's data beats a generalist trained on everything, on that domain. It is a real, named effect: *negative transfer* or *task interference*. A [vision-language study](#c/vl-study) found that task experts trained on the relevant subset beat the all-data model on 5 of 7 tasks. An expert-LM paper reported +10.4% mean accuracy from picking task experts over a multi-task baseline. Labs' practice points the same way: several open reasoning models [specialize, then merge](#c/merging) by weight-averaging. Positive transfer pushes the other way. Math training improved coding, data-poor tasks free-ride on data-rich ones, and one study found transfer is asymmetric: code and math are "safe donors," factuality is an "intrusive" one. Most specialist-wins evidence is from SFT and smaller or vision-language settings, and very large models seem to absorb diverse tasks with less interference. **Status: contested.** It likely holds more for small models and narrow budgets.

c-data-lever.overview: **Claim:** data curation (sourcing, cleaning, [deduplication](#c/dedup), [model-based quality filtering](#c/quality-filter), mixing, [decontamination](#c/decontamination)) is the single biggest lever on model quality, and probably the largest share of effort. The key evidence is the [DCLM benchmark](#c/dclm). It holds architecture and training fixed, varies only the curation, and found that keeping just the top ~10% of Common Crawl by a small classifier let a 7B model reach 64% MMLU on 2.6T tokens, beating the prior open-data best by about 6 MMLU points at half the compute. That field-wide benchmarks now compete on curation is itself a signal. Post-training reports (Motif, [Tülu 3](#c/tulu3)) name dataset construction as the hardest part, and teams reuse existing mixtures rather than build their own. Against it: no rigorous effort-share figure exists ("80% is data" is folklore), and the evidence is from open-data projects, not closed flagships. **Status: emerging.**

c-hybrid-parity.overview: **Claim:** [Mamba–Transformer hybrids](#c/hybrids) match pure transformers' quality at large scale, with better efficiency. For it: [Jamba](#c/jamba) scales to 398B and is competitive on standard and long-context benchmarks. [Granite 4.0](#c/granite-4)'s H-Small beat every open model on IFEval except one twelve times its size. Nemotron-H is described as state-of-the-art with faster inference. Much of this is [vendor-reported](#c/vendor-claims) on favourable benchmarks. Against it: Jamba shows known SSM weaknesses in reasoning and code, so parity is average rather than uniform. A 2026 [robustness paper](#c/robustness-paper) found that hybrids collapse under hidden-state-poisoning triggers that don't affect pure transformers, one early paper on one attack class. No hybrid leads the overall frontier, which remains transformer-based as far as is known. **Status: emerging.** It is a Pareto win (comparable quality, less memory, more speed), not yet a strict capability tie everywhere.

c-diffusion-parity.overview: **Claim:** [diffusion language models](#c/diffusion-lm) reach the quality of autoregressive models while generating 5–10× faster. For it: [Gemini Diffusion](#c/gemini-diffusion) roughly matches Gemini 2.0 Flash Lite on code (HumanEval 89.6% vs 90.2%, MBPP 76.0% vs 75.8%) at about 5× the speed. [Mercury Coder](#c/mercury) reports coding parity at 5–10× the throughput of comparable AR models, and Mercury 2 posts strong AIME and LiveCodeBench scores. All of these numbers are the vendors' own, and all are in code and maths, structured domains. Against it: the May 2026 ["No Free Lunch" survey](#c/no-free-lunch) compares dLLM inference acceleration with AR models under controlled conditions and finds that the speedups come with trade-offs the headline tokens/s hide. Structural issues remain around variable-length output and KV-caching. No dLLM claims to be the best model overall. **Status: contested.** The claim holds for coding on vendor benchmarks, and general parity is unproven.

c-glm52.overview: **Claim:** Zhipu's [GLM-5.2](#c/glm-52), released June 13, 2026, beats GPT-5.5 on several long-horizon coding benchmarks at about one-sixth the cost. The evidence conflicts across time. [Launch coverage from June 13–15](#c/glm52-early) says no official scores were published at release, with no SWE-bench Verified, LiveCodeBench or HumanEval, and treats the numbers as marketing promises. [Later coverage from June 16–17](#c/glm52-late) carries strong claims: 753B open weights beating GPT-5.5, and even outperforming Claude Opus 4.7 and, in some blind tests, Claude Fable 5. That wave appeared only in aggregated coverage and contradicts the earlier reports. Its sourcing is unclear and vendor-flavoured, and it landed during a charged moment tied to US restrictions on American models abroad. There is no technical report yet. What is confirmed about 5.2 is a 1M-token context and High/Max reasoning modes. **Status: contested.** Wait for independent evaluation.

m-layers.overview: **Myth:** every layer of a transformer guesses the next token, and the model blends those guesses. It is a natural picture. "Deep" suggests many parallel judgments, ensembles of voters are a familiar way to improve predictions, and interpretability tools like the logit lens *can* read rough early guesses from middle layers. In reality the layers form a sequential pipeline. Each layer transforms one vector per token and adds its adjustment to the [residual stream](#c/residual), and only after the last layer does the [output head](#c/output-head) turn that vector into a probability distribution. There is exactly one prediction. It is "an assembly line, not a panel of voters." Early exit and logit lens are diagnostic or optimization tricks, not how normal inference works. See [the correction](#c/r-layers).

r-layers.overview: In a standard [decoder-only transformer](#c/transformer), a token enters as an embedding vector and passes up the [layer stack](#c/layer-stack). Each layer applies attention, the only place tokens exchange information, then a feed-forward network that works on each token independently. Both are wrapped in residual connections, so each layer *adds an adjustment* to a running representation, the [residual stream](#c/residual), rather than replacing it. Early layers tend to capture local, surface patterns, and later ones more abstract, long-range structure. Only the final layer's output goes through the unembedding [output head](#c/output-head) to become a next-token distribution. Every layer also has its own independently learned query, key and value heads and its own FFN, which is why depth adds representational power rather than repetition. It is also why the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) is stored per layer.

m-sonnet.overview: **Myth:** Epoch's "inference cost falls ~100× per year" means a specific model, say a particular Sonnet, gets 100× cheaper to run each year. It is an easy reading. The headline is phrased as "the cost of inference," and prices of named models do sometimes drop. But the metric fixes *capability*, not the model. It tracks the cheapest model that clears a given benchmark bar, and that model changes over time: a task that needed GPT-4-class compute in 2023 might be handled by something Haiku-sized later. See [cost at a fixed capability](#c/fixed-capability). A frozen set of weights does get cheaper to serve, through [serving optimizations](#c/serving-opts) like batching, quantization and better kernels, and through [new hardware generations](#c/hardware-gens). That happens at a far more modest pace and in lumps. And the [price you pay](#c/price-vs-cost) is a business decision only loosely tied to either.

m-harder.overview: **Myth:** as benchmark bars rise, it should take cheap models longer and longer to catch up, so cost declines should be slowest at the top. It sounds airtight, since harder capability seems harder to reproduce cheaply. The data shows the opposite. In the [price-trend paper](#c/price-paper), the top GPQA-Diamond bin fell 31× per year and the bottom bin only 1.7×. See [Price declines are fastest at the capability frontier](#c/c-frontier-fastest). The reason is headroom. A newly reached bar is at first cleared only by one expensive model, so the first cheaper model to match it is a huge multiplier, often via [distillation](#c/distillation) or MoE. Old low bars have already had their cost wrung out. The user's instinct does survive in another form: the steepest drops are recent, and Epoch warns they may not persist.

m-carbon.overview: **Myth:** the "lossy" caveat on the claude-carbon tool means its token *cost* figures are unreliable. That's a reasonable worry when a tracking tool warns about lossiness and you only care about dollars. But the caveat is about its carbon estimates. The token counts and dollar costs come straight from Claude Code's own JSONL transcripts, the same data that ccusage, the built-in `/cost` command and the status line read, so they are equally accurate across all of them. The lossy part is converting tokens into grams of CO₂. That relies on extrapolated per-model emission factors, counts cache reads at full rate, and assumes average grid carbon intensity, because Anthropic doesn't publish per-model energy data. See [the correction](#c/r-carbon). For [serving cost](#c/cost-per-token) and energy more broadly, only estimates exist.

r-carbon.overview: For tracking what Claude Code sessions cost, the token counts and dollar figures are exact. Every tool reads the same local transcripts (`~/.claude` JSONL logs), so claude-carbon, ccusage (the standard answer, with per-day, per-session and per-project breakdowns and a live mode), the built-in `/cost` command and the status line all agree. On Pro/Max subscriptions `/cost` shows tokens but not dollars, since those plans aren't billed per token. What is genuinely lossy is claude-carbon's conversion of tokens into CO₂. It uses extrapolated emission factors for models without published data, counts cache reads at full rate, and assumes grid-average carbon intensity. That won't be "fixed," because Anthropic doesn't publish per-model energy data. Treat the carbon figure as order-of-magnitude. See [the misconception](#c/m-carbon) and, for why per-token [serving cost](#c/cost-per-token) is itself opaque, [Price ≠ serving cost](#c/price-vs-cost).

m-experts.overview: **Myth:** in a [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) model, each expert is a topic specialist. A chemistry question goes to the "chemistry expert," a coding question to the coding one. The name invites this, and it matches how human teams divide work. In reality an expert is just one of many parallel [feed-forward](#c/ffn) weight blocks inside a layer. The [router](#c/router) is a small linear layer that scores every expert with a dot product against the token's current vector and sends the token to the top few. That decision is re-made for every token at every MoE layer, so neighbouring words can go to entirely different experts. When researchers inspect trained routers, specialization is mostly low-level and syntactic (punctuation, numbers, structural roles), not human topics. See [the correction](#c/r-experts).

r-experts.overview: MoE routing is fine-grained and mechanical. At each MoE layer, a small [router](#c/router) computes a score for every expert as a dot product between the token's current vector and each expert's learned routing vector. A softmax turns the scores into weights, and the token goes to the top-k experts, whose outputs are combined by those weights. The decision is made fresh for every token at every layer: a 60-layer model makes 60 routing decisions per token, and the active set churns constantly. Inspected routers show experts specializing in low-level, often syntactic or positional patterns rather than topics. Training needs [load balancing](#c/lb-loss) to stop a few experts from winning everything, and designs like DeepSeek's [shared expert](#c/shared-expert-c) handle common processing. The payoff is that the full pool of [routed experts](#c/experts) sets capacity, while only the few active ones set per-token cost.

m-gpu.overview: **Myth:** AI capacity is simply a matter of how many GPUs exist. It's natural, because Nvidia dominates the headlines and accelerators are the most expensive visible component. In reality the [binding constraint](#c/capacity) has kept moving. Through 2024 and early 2025 it was [power](#c/power): Microsoft reportedly held chips it couldn't plug in. By late 2025 it swung back to chip supply. By around May 2026 it was [transformers and switchgear](#c/electrical-gear), with high-voltage transformer lead times of 36–48 months. [HBM memory](#c/hbm-supply) is the underappreciated one. It was sold out for 2026 and is heading toward about 30% of hyperscaler AI spend, up from about 8%. On top of that, 30–50% of planned 2026 data-center capacity is projected to slip to 2028. At least four constraints bind in turn, so buying more GPUs alone doesn't add capacity.

m-bigger.overview: **Myth:** frontier models keep getting bigger in parameter count. It was true for years. GPT-1 to GPT-3 grew about 1,000× in two years, and GPT-3 to GPT-4 (an estimated 1.8T) another ~10×. Extrapolation would put today's models near 10 trillion. But in 2023 the trend reversed. Epoch estimates GPT-4o at about 200B and Claude 3.5 Sonnet at about 400B, roughly an order of magnitude smaller than GPT-4. These are estimates: Anthropic has never published a parameter count. [Chinchilla scaling](#c/chinchilla) showed models had been too big for their data, and [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) split total parameters from the active parameters that set cost. Capability now rides on training compute, data, [algorithmic efficiency](#c/algorithmic-progress) and test-time compute. See [the correction](#c/r-smaller).

r-smaller.overview: Parameter count and capability decoupled around 2023. Before then, scaling meant making dense models bigger: [GPT-3](#c/gpt-3) at 175B, then [GPT-4](#c/gpt-4) at an estimated ~1.8T. After GPT-4, Epoch estimates that frontier models like GPT-4o (~200B) and Claude 3.5 Sonnet (~400B) were about an order of magnitude *smaller*. Those are estimates, not disclosures. Two forces explain it. [Chinchilla](#c/chinchilla) showed that for a fixed budget it pays to train smaller models on far more data. [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) made "parameter count" ambiguous: [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) has 671B total but only 37B active per token, giving big-model capacity at small-model running cost. Open-weight totals have since climbed back into the hundreds of billions and low trillions while active counts stay low. That decoupling is part of why inference keeps getting cheaper at a fixed capability.

m-moe-new.overview: **Myth:** Mixture of Experts is a recent breakthrough, arriving around the time of Mixtral and DeepSeek. It feels new because MoE only became the dominant open architecture from 2024, and that is when it entered public conversation about cheaper, bigger models. In fact the idea is old. It dates to 1991 with ["Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts"](#c/moe-1991). The [sparsely-gated layer](#c/sparse-moe) that matters for LLMs came in 2017, the same year as the Transformer, followed by [GShard](#c/gshard) (2020) and [Switch Transformer](#c/switch) (2021). What turned it into the backbone of frontier models was a decade of incremental fixes, not a sudden invention. The Epoch price data starts around 2024, so it captures MoE's spread, not its arrival. See [the correction](#c/r-moe-old).

r-moe-old.overview: Mixture of Experts has a long history. Jacobs, Hinton, Jordan and Nowlan proposed [adaptive mixtures of local experts](#c/moe-1991) in 1991. Shazeer and colleagues at Google published the [sparsely-gated MoE layer](#c/sparse-moe) in 2017, enabling 137B-parameter networks by activating only a few experts per input. GShard brought it into the Transformer in 2020, scaling past 600B, and Switch Transformer in 2021 simplified routing to one expert per token. Yet little of the value was realized at invention. It came from years of fixes: [load-balancing losses](#c/lb-loss), capacity limits, routing stability, fine-grained and shared experts, [auxiliary-loss-free balancing](#c/aux-free) and systems work for expert parallelism. That history is the chat's main example for the claim that [sustained cost declines come mostly from incremental work](#c/c-incremental).

m-price.overview: **Myth:** what you pay per token tracks what it costs the provider to serve that token, so falling serving costs show up as falling prices. It's a natural assumption from competitive markets, and prices *do* fall over time. But the API price is a business decision only loosely coupled to cost. Prices usually hold flat across a model's life and then drop in a step when a successor launches, even if [serving cost](#c/cost-per-token) fell gradually in between through better batching, quantization, kernels and hardware. Proprietary vendors also rarely cut old models' list prices, which is one reason the all-models ["100×/year"](#c/c-100x) figure is inflated. Scarcity pushes the other way: premium models like Fable 5 are priced and metered because [frontier capacity is scarce](#c/frontier-price). See [Price ≠ serving cost](#c/price-vs-cost).

m-distill.overview: **Claude's own overreach:** early in the chat, Claude said that "a chunk of apparent 'reasoning gains' may be [distillation](#c/distillation) from stronger models doing the heavy lifting." It was an easy step to make. The [RLVR coverage study](#c/rlvr-study) Claude was summarizing had contrasted RL, which mostly sharpens existing ability, with distillation, which can transfer new reasoning. And distillation from closed models really was pervasive in open chat models. When the user pressed for evidence, Claude separated three claims. Distillation works: established. It is widespread in open models: well supported. It explains a chunk of the headline *reasoning* gains: not supported by any measurement. The flagship counterexample is [DeepSeek-R1](#c/deepseek-r1), whose reasoning came from [RLVR](#c/rlvr) and was then distilled downward into its own smaller models. Claude retracted the confident version. See [the correction](#c/r-distill).

r-distill.overview: What the evidence supports: [distillation](#c/distillation), meaning training a model on a stronger model's outputs, is proven and powerful. It was the dominant way the 2023–24 open wave (Alpaca, Open Orca, ShareGPT) got its chat quality, and even [Tülu 3](#c/tulu3) generates its SFT responses with GPT-4o and Claude. It can transfer reasoning too, and DeepSeek used it to spread [R1](#c/deepseek-r1)'s reasoning into smaller models. What the evidence does *not* support is that distilling closed frontier models secretly drives the headline open-model reasoning gains. The best-documented case got its reasoning from [RLVR](#c/rlvr). No reliable share can be measured, because labs don't disclose post-training data and using competitors' outputs often violates terms of service, so the signals (models claiming to be ChatGPT, similar output distributions) stay circumstantial. See the contested claim that [distillation drives open reasoning gains](#c/c-distill-open).
